verses.143:1: Bendito o Senhor, meu Deus, que {docet} as minhas mãos para a batalha, * e os meus dedos para a guerra.
verses.143:2: A minha misericórdia, e o meu refúgio: * o meu amparo, e o meu {liberator}:
verses.143:2b: O meu protetor, e nele esperei: * {subdit} o meu povo sob mim.
verses.143:3: Senhor, que é o homem, {quia3a} {innotuisti}? * ou o filho do homem, {quia3b} {reputas}?
verses.143:4: O homem {factus} semelhante {vanitati}: * os seus dias passam como a sombra.
verses.143:5: Senhor, inclinai os vossos céus, e descei: * tocai os montes, e fumegarão.
verses.143:6: {fulgura}, e os dispersareis: * enviai as vossas setas, e os perturbareis.
verses.143:7: Enviai a vossa mão do alto, {eripe7}, e livrai-me {aquis}: * da mão dos {alieni7}.
verses.143:8: Cuja boca {locutum8} {vanitatem8}: * e a sua direita é direita de iniquidade.
verses.143:9: Deus, eu vos cantarei um cântico novo: * com o saltério de dez cordas vos entoarei salmos.
verses.143:10: Vós que dais a salvação aos reis: * que resgatastes Davi, vosso servo, da espada {maligno}: {eripe10}.
verses.143:11: E {erue11} da mão dos {alieni11}, cuja boca {locutum11} {vanitatem11}: * e a sua direita é direita de iniquidade:
verses.143:12: Cujos filhos são como {plantationes} * na sua juventude.
verses.143:14: Não há ruína de {maceria}, nem {transitus}: * nem clamor nas suas praças.
verses.143:15: {beatum} o povo que tem estas coisas: * bem-aventurado o povo cujo Deus é o Senhor.

decisions.latin: éripe me, et líbera me de aquis multis (7) · éripe me (10) · Et érue me de manu filiórum alienórum (11)
decisions.why: Three Latin rescue verbs in five verses: erípere (7, 10), liberáre (7), érue (11). The glossary splits erípere by source — 'arrancar' where a 'de …' follows, 'libertar' where none is named — and gives éruere 'arrancar' with a source; liberáre is 'livrar'. 143:7 has a source after the pair (de aquis multis), so 'arrancai-me, e livrai-me' — as 81:4, where draft 1's 'libertai … livrai' drew a Latinist minor for sounding like one verb. 143:10 ends 'éripe me.' with no source (de gládio malígno belongs to redemísti, DO's colon) → 'libertai-me', as 118:153, 118:170, 68:19. 143:11 'érue me de manu' → 'arrancai-me'. So where éripe (10) and érue (11) touch, the Portuguese keeps them apart; the cost is that éripe (7) and érue (11), in two nearly identical lines, share 'arrancai-me'. Option 2 keeps éripe one verb inside the psalm at the price of the 'libertai … livrai' chime. v1 Latinist (minor) asked 'arrancai-me' at 143:10 for one Portuguese verb per éripe; refused: with no source named 'arrancai-me' hangs (the row's Ps 6 / 118:153 finding), and it would merge éripe (10) with érue (11) where the two Latin verbs touch. His reading is option 3. The v2 Latinist repeated the minor, now proposing 'arrancai-me' at 10 and 'tirai-me' for érue at 11; held — 'tirar' belongs to edúcere and auferre, and 'arrancai-me' with nothing to be torn from is the row's recorded failure. Option 4.

options.label: arrancai-me (7) · libertai-me (10) · arrancai-me (11)
options.note: Draft. The glossary's rule by source (erípere and éruere rows; 81:4, 30:3/30:16).

options.label: libertai-me (7) · libertai-me (10) · arrancai-me (11)
options.note: One Portuguese verb per Latin verb inside the psalm (as 70:1 'livrai-me, e libertai-me'); 'libertai-me, e livrai-me' chimes, the 81:4 objection.

options.label: arrancai-me (7) · arrancai-me (10) · arrancai-me (11)
options.note: One verb throughout; at 10 'arrancai-me' hangs with nothing to be torn from (the row's Ps 6 / 118:153 finding).

options.label: arrancai-me (7) · arrancai-me (10) · tirai-me (11)
options.note: The v2 Latinist: éripe one verb, érue kept apart with 'tirar' — which is edúcere's (106:28) and auferre's (D41) in this psalter.

decisions.why: The liberátor row (working: libertador) notes a crossing: the noun sits in erípere's Portuguese family (libertar) while liberáre is 'livrar', and asks Ps 143 to decide, since this psalm has both verbs (143:7 líbera → livrai-me; 143:10 éripe → libertai-me). 'Livrador' is not current Portuguese; 'salvador' is salvátor's. Kept: the crossing is between verses eight apart and no Portuguese agent noun of 'livrar' exists. It also serves the Vespers antiphon 'Benedíctus Dóminus * suscéptor meus et liberátor meus' (Psalmi major, Saturday Vespers), which reads 'Bendito o Senhor, * o meu amparo e o meu libertador'. Same as 17:2, 17:48, 69:6b.

options.label: livrador
options.note: Keeps liberáre's family; not a current word.

decisions.latin: quid est homo, quia innotuísti ei?
decisions.why: The near-twin of 8:5 (Quid est homo quod memor es ejus), whose Portuguese builds the question 'que é o homem, para que …?' with a subjunctive — held against the Latinist there (D25) because it is how Portuguese asks this question. Built the same way here so the two verses sound kin. innotéscere is 'become known' (ἐγνώσθης αὐτῷ, 'you made yourself known to him'; DRB 'thou art made known to him'); 'dar-se a conhecer' says exactly that, and the perfect is kept (innotuísti). MS1932 'te tenhas manifestado' uses another word.

options.label: a ele vos tenhais dado a conhecer

forms.innotuisti: a ele vos tenhais dado a conhecer

options.note: v2, the stylist's order: the colon lands on the stressed end of 'conhecer' instead of a weak 'a ele'. Order only (D2).

options.label: vos tenhais dado a conhecer a ele

forms.innotuisti: vos tenhais dado a conhecer a ele

options.label: vos deis a conhecer a ele

forms.innotuisti: vos deis a conhecer a ele

decisions.latin: aut fílius hóminis, quia réputas eum?
decisions.why: reputáre, to reckon, take into account (λογίζῃ αὐτόν; DRB 'makest account of him'). 'Levar em conta' is the plain Portuguese for it, present as the Latin. 'Ter em conta' would echo 'tenhais' of the first colon (a jingle the Latin, innotuísti … réputas, does not have); 118:119 reputávi → 'Tive por' is another sense (to hold someone as). MS1932 'estimares' means esteem, which is narrower.

decisions.latin: vanitáti símilis (4) · os locútum est vanitátem (8, 11)
decisions.why: The vánitas row (working: vaidade) has been heard as conceit by blind readers in Pss 4/118, 30, 37, 39, 61, and flags 'o que é vão' for the coordinator. Kept to the row: vaidade is the Latin's word, the three places here repeat it (8 = 11 word for word), and 143:4 'semelhante à vaidade' is the Latin's image of emptiness (ματαιότητι). MS1932 has 'ao nada' at 4 (a paraphrase; his 'vaidade' at 8, 11). If the row moves, the three slots move together.

options.label: o que é vão
options.note: The row's candidate for the coordinator.

options.label: ao nada / vaidade
options.note: MS1932 at 4; splits one Latin word.

decisions.why: The same phrase as the refrain 48:13 = 48:21 'símilis factus est illis' → 'se fez semelhante a eles', so the same Portuguese (rule 6). The fíeri row keeps 'tornar-se' for a state come upon the subject (118:83, 13:1b), which is arguably the sense here; but the identical Latin phrase governs.

An imperative verb (fulguráre) with a noun object (coruscátio), 'flash forth a flash'; the Greek ἄστραψον ἀστραπήν is one root twice, the Latin varies it. The coruscátio row has 'relâmpago' (76:19, as fúlgur 17:15, 96:4) and says 143:6 needs its own look. Portuguese 'fulgurar' is intransitive, so 'Fazei fulgurar o relâmpago' keeps both the verb's root and the noun. 'Fazei brilhar' is plainer but makes lightning merely shine. 'Relampejai o relâmpago' would copy the Greek's figure, which the Latin does not have. v2: the stylist asked 'brilhar' and the ambiguity reader did not know 'fulgurar'; taken as the plainer of two faithful words — both render a verb of flashing light, and 'relâmpago' carries the lightning.

options.label: Fazei brilhar o relâmpago
options.note: v2, the stylist's: the plainer of two faithful verbs (D2); 'fulgurar' was unknown to the ambiguity reader and bookish to the stylist. MS1932 'Faze brilhar'.

options.label: Fazei fulgurar o relâmpago
options.note: v1. Keeps the root of fulguráre.

decisions.why: D24 settled malígnus → 'malvado' because 'o maligno' as a noun was heard as the devil. Here it is an adjective on a sword, where that hearing cannot arise, and 'espada malvada' puts a word for wicked people on a thing. 'maligna' (MS1932) keeps the Latin's word; πονηρᾶς is 'evil'.

The novéllæ row (rebentos, 127:3b 'como rebentos de oliveiras') says 143:12 will test it; the Greek is the same νεόφυτα. But the Latin differs: at 127:3 novéllæ is the noun, here it is an adjective on plantatiónes, so rule 6 does not bind. 'Plantas novas' keeps both words in their roles; it is also MS1932's and the Ave Maria's phrase (circulation.md). 'Plantações' would be heard as plantations.

options.label: rebentos plantados
options.note: Echoes 127:3b's 'rebentos'; the noun turned participle. 'rebentos' was unknown to one reader.

options.label: novas plantações
options.note: The cognate; heard as fields of crops.

decisions.why: compósitus, 'well arranged, adorned' (L&S); the Greek κεκαλλωπισμέναι is 'made beautiful'. Portuguese 'compostas' now says 'composed, decent' (MS1932 'andam todas compostas' has the older sense). 'Enfeitadas' is the plain word for the Greek's sense and sets up the second colon's 'adornadas' (circumornátæ), two words of adornment as in the Latin.

options.label: bem compostas
options.note: The cognate, with 'bem' against the modern sense; MS1932 'compostas'.

decisions.why: 'ut similitúdo templi', 'as the likeness of a temple' (ὁμοίωμα ναοῦ; DRB 'after the similitude of a temple'). 'À semelhança de' is the living Portuguese for it and keeps the noun (105:20 'semelhança'); a literal 'como a semelhança de' is not a sentence (the similitúdo row, 57:5). The Hebrew's 'columns / pillars of the temple' (Ave Maria, CNBB) is another text. MS1932's 'como ídolos dum templo' is a gloss. v2: a comma before it, from the stylist's line (breath).

options.label: como a imagem de um templo

forms.similitudo: como a imagem de um templo

decisions.why: The eructáre row: 'fazer jorrar' (18:3, 44:2a, 118:171), the gush kept, the belch not; 143:13 is one of its five places. Here the participle has no object, so the verb's intransitive 'jorrando' keeps the root without 'fazer'. 'ex hoc in illud' → 'deste para aquele', as 74:9 'ex hoc in hoc' → 'deste para aquele'. MS1932 'a trasbordar duns para outros' is another image (overflowing). v2: the stylist asked 'transbordando' (jorrar of grain odd) — refused, the row's root kept; option 1.

The sheep 'abounding in their goings-out' (πληθύνοντα ἐν ταῖς ἐξόδοις αὐτῶν; DRB 'abounding in their goings forth'). egréssio is 'saída' at 18:6b. Kept as noun and adjective; MS1932 turns it into a clause and adds 'a pastar'.

The Latin adjective is feminine (crassæ), so the animals are cows; the Greek (οἱ βόες … παχεῖς) is masculine, and DRB says 'oxen'. Rule 1: the Latin. MS1932 reads it so: 'As suas vacas são gordas'. The cost: 8:8 and 49:10 have 'bois' for boves (no gender marked there).

decisions.latin: Non est ruína macériæ, neque tránsitus
decisions.why: tránsitus (διέξοδος) is left bare in the Latin: a passage through the broken wall, or a going-out (into exile, or of the flock). 'Nem passagem' keeps it as open as the Latin (DRB 'nor passage', MS1932 'nem passagem na sua cerca' with a gloss). macéria → 'cerca' as 61:4, 79:13; ruína as 105:29.

options.label: brecha
options.note: Decides the sense (a hole in the wall); DM1962's word is for the Hebrew's first noun.

decisions.latin: Beátum dixérunt pópulum, cui hæc sunt
decisions.why: The Latin opens both cola on 'beátus' (Beátum … beátus), and the second colon is the Saturday Vespers antiphon 'Beátus pópulus * cujus Dóminus Deus ejus', which must read alone. Setting 'disseram' between commas keeps the anaphora and the Latin's order; 'Chamaram bem-aventurado o povo' is plainer but buries the first 'bem-aventurado'. The 'but' of MS1932's gloss '(eu porém digo)' is not in the Latin and not added: the contrast is left to the reader, as the Latin leaves it. 'Cujo Deus é o Senhor' = 32:12 'Beáta gens, cujus est Dóminus, Deus ejus' → 'Bem-aventurada a nação cujo Deus é o Senhor'; it is also the Ave Maria's and the Almeida's wording (circulation.md). 'Cui hæc sunt' → 'que tem estas coisas' (possession, plainly).

options.label: Bem-aventurado, disseram,
options.note: Draft; the Latin's order and anaphora.

options.label: Chamaram bem-aventurado
options.note: Plainer order; DRB 'They have called the people happy'.

decisions.latin: quia innotuísti ei? … quia réputas eum?
decisions.why: The Latinist (v1, minor) reads 'quia' as a plain 'that' and hears a purpose in 'para que'. The same question in 8:5 (quod memor es … quóniam vísitas) is built 'que é o homem, para que …?' and was held there against two Latinist majors (D25): it is how Portuguese asks this question, presupposing the fact, and MS1932 builds it the same way here ('para que a ele te tenhas manifestado'). His fix 'que é o homem, que vos tenhais dado a conhecer a ele?' is not a Portuguese question. Refused; kept as an option.

decisions.latin: qui docet manus meas ad prǽlium
decisions.why: The same Latin as 17:35 'Qui docet manus meas ad prǽlium' → 'Que ensina as minhas mãos para a batalha', so the same Portuguese (rule 6). The stylist asks 'adestra' (the CNBB's verb, from the Hebrew לְמַד too — circulation.md): 'ensinar … para' is a calque to him. Refused: docére → ensinar is the row's (17:35–36b echo 'ensina … me ensinará'), and the Ps 17 stylist's 'instrui' was refused for the same reason. If taken, 17:35 moves with it.

options.label: adestra
options.note: The v1 stylist; MS1932 'adestra' too. Another verb (train).

decisions.latin: qui subdit pópulum meum sub me
decisions.why: The stylist heard the bare 'que' as having lost its antecedent (the titles are two cola back) and 'que sujeita' as possibly 'que [é] sujeita'; the ambiguity reader heard the same loose 'que' and 'sujeita' as an adjective. Naming the subject is grammar (D2) and settles both; the verb stays 17:48's.

The same Latin as 17:17 'assúmpsit me de aquis multis' → 'de muitas águas' (rule 6; 76:20, 106:23 'em muitas águas'). The stylist hears it clipped and asks 'das muitas águas' (MS1932's). The article is grammar and D2 would allow it, but it would break a phrase that stands three times; refused, option — if taken, taken in 17:17 too.

The aliénus row keeps 'estranho' (wider than 'estrangeiro': anyone not one's own), and 17:46 'Os filhos estranhos' was held after a blind reader heard 'odd children'. Here the stylist and the ambiguity reader both heard 'strange, odd children' again — the second psalm with that finding, recorded in the row for the coordinator. Held for the row and the Ps 17 twin; 'filhos estrangeiros' (the stylist) and 'filhos de estrangeiros' (17:46's option) are options, both slots together.

options.label: filhos estrangeiros
options.note: The v1 stylist. Narrows aliénus to foreigners.

decisions.why: loqui → 'falar', with the accusative of content kept, as 37:13 'falaram vaidades', 16:9b 'falou soberba', 121:8 'falava paz' (the loqui pacem row). The stylist asks 'proferiu' as more idiomatic with an abstract object. Refused: another verb for the Latin's plain 'speak', and it would split this formula from its kin. Option.

The stylist found 'adornadas em volta' stiff and 'volta à' a clump, and asked 'ornadas em redor,' with a comma for breath. Taken: same meaning, 'ornar' is nearer circum-ornáre than 'adornar', and 'em redor' is the Latin's 'circum'.

The stylist heard 'deste para aquele' dangling with no noun and asked 'de um para outro', the Portuguese idiom; the ambiguity reader could not place 'deste para aquele' either. Taken: the idiom says 'from this one into that one' as the Latin does. 74:9's 'ex hoc in hoc' → 'deste para aquele' is not the same Latin (a cup poured), so rule 6 does not bind. His 'transbordando' was refused (the eructantia decision).

options.label: de um para outro
options.note: v2, the stylist's; MS1932 'duns para outros'.

decisions.why: macéria → 'cerca' is the row's (61:4, 79:13; φραγμός). The stylist hears a fence and asks 'muro' (MS1932 'ruína de muro'); the ambiguity reader could mishear 'cerca' as 'cerca de' (about). L&S macéria is a wall of loose stones, an enclosure. Held for the row and its two psalms; 'muro' is murus's word elsewhere. Evidence added to the row.

choices.143:1: Head as the formula 'Bendito o Senhor, Deus de Israel' (40:14, 71:18; D41) — no 'seja'. The rest copies 17:35 'Que ensina as minhas mãos para a batalha' (prǽlium → batalha, bellum → guerra, as 17:40, 75:4). Also the Gradual of 03-27 (missa Sancti). No titulus (D7: DO's Psalm143.txt has none; the Greek's τῷ Δαυιδ πρὸς τὸν Γολιαδ and MS1932's 'Salmo de David, contra Golias' are not in the working text).
choices.143:2: Verbless appositions, as 17:3c 'O meu protetor, e o chifre da minha salvação, * e o meu amparo'; article kept before each possessive. suscéptor → amparo (D19). The first Vespers antiphon (Benedíctus Dóminus * suscéptor meus et liberátor meus) is built from these words: 'Bendito o Senhor, * o meu amparo e o meu libertador'.
choices.143:2b: 'qui subdit pópulum meum sub me' follows 17:48 'sujeitais os povos sob mim' (subdere takes subjícere's verb; the row says 143:2 should follow). 'nele esperei' as 27:7.
choices.143:4: 'como a sombra', with the article, as 101:12 and 108:23. prætéreunt → 'passam'.
choices.143:5: 17:10 'Inclinou os céus, e desceu' and 103:32 'que toca os montes, e eles fumegam' — the same verbs. 'descei', 'tocai' are safe at the vós imperative (past 'desci', 'toquei').
choices.143:6: dissipáre with people as object → 'dispersar' (the row's proposal, 17:15 'e os dispersou', 67:31b 'Dispersai'); conturbáre → 'perturbar' (17:15). emíttere → 'enviar', one verb for 143:6 and 143:7 (the emíttere row; 17:15, 17:17 'enviou'). The ambiguity reader found no antecedent for 'os' (dispersareis, perturbareis): the Latin's 'eos' has none either (the enemies appear in 143:7); kept.
choices.143:7: 'de muitas águas' without the article, as 17:17 'de muitas águas'; 'da mão dos filhos estranhos' as the aliénus row (17:46 'Os filhos estranhos'). The Latin order 'a vossa mão do alto' kept.
choices.143:8: Relative 'Cuja' opens the verse and hangs on 143:7, as the Latin's 'Quorum'. A copula is supplied in the second colon (the Latin has none); the repeated 'direita' kept. déxtera → 'direita' (row). 143:11 repeats 143:8 word for word, as the Latin does. The ambiguity reader heard 'direita' without 'mão' as 'what is right' or the political right: the déxtera row keeps the bare noun, as 17:36a, 117:16; recorded, not changed.
choices.143:9: The responsory of Pasc4-0 (R. Deus, cánticum novum cantábo tibi … In psaltério decem chordárum psallam tibi) reads from this verse. psaltério decachórdo → 'o saltério de dez cordas' (32:2; the decachórdum row names 143:9 for this). psállere → 'entoar salmos' (D25), 'vos entoarei salmos' as 137:1b. Bare vocative 'Deus' (D44).
choices.143:10: salus → 'salvação' (D6); MS1932's 'saúde' is the older sense. redímere perfect → 'resgatastes' (the row: 30:6, 70:23, 76:15). 'Davi, vosso servo' as 131:10. The LXX ends 143:10 at πονηρᾶς and has ῥῦσαί με in 143:11; the Latin moves 'éripe me' to the end of 10 — kept there.
choices.143:12: 'Quorum' refers back to the 'filhos estranhos' (143:11), as in the Greek (ὧν): in the Latin, 143:12–14 describe the prosperity of the strangers, and 143:15a reports that men called such a people happy. The Hebrew (and so the CNBB and Ave Maria, circulation.md) reads 'our sons … our barns' as a wish; not followed. Copulas supplied at the head of 12, 12b, 13, 13b (grammar, D2); the second cola stay verbless as in the Latin.
choices.143:15: The second colon is the Saturday Vespers antiphon 'Beátus pópulus * cujus Dóminus Deus ejus' (Psalmi major) and reads alone: 'Bem-aventurado o povo * cujo Deus é o Senhor'. beátus → 'bem-aventurado' (D19). The ambiguity reader could not tell who 'disseram' are and heard both lines as one approving statement: the Latin leaves it just so (no 'sed'); kept.

audit.note: Psalm-level draft from consult/parallels/ps143.md, with precedent from ps143/concord.py over all finished psalms (Ps 17's twin lines, 8:5, 48:13, 32:12, 74:9, 101:12, 103:32, 127:3b) and the glossary rows. Brazilian circulation of the closing verses fetched, not asserted: ps143/circulation.md. Liturgical uses found by grep in DO's Latin: two Saturday Vespers antiphons (143:1–2, 143:15b), the Pasc4-0 responsory (143:9), a Gradual (03-27, 143:1). Hard readings: the three rescue verbs (7, 10, 11); fulgura coruscatiónem; the Latin's 'quorum' making 12–14 the strangers' prosperity against the Hebrew's wish; boves … crassæ (feminine).

Hard checks pass. Soft flags accepted: 143:3 +6 (the counter does not elide; sung, 'que‿é‿o … dado‿a … a‿ele' is ~18 against 16, and the 8:5 build needs the auxiliary; 'vos deis a conhecer' is the shorter option); 143:15 +5 (same elisions; the anaphora kept); 143:9 +3 (the 32:2 formula); 143:12b +3; short second cola at 143:7, 143:14 and first cola at 143:11, 143:12 (-3 to -6), where the Latin's long words have short Portuguese equivalents. Rhymes inside 143:6 (-reis/-reis) and 143:8 = 143:11 (vaidade/iniquidade) are the Latin's own echoes (dissipábis eos / conturbábis eos; vanitátem / iniquitátis).
